original_question: Determine whether fundamental constants vary with time, in particular whether the gravitational constant should remain fixed only in static situations and vary in dynamical ones according to a reproducible rule that agrees with astronomical and laboratory observations.
target_in_paper: Section 7.7, "Do fundamental constants in Nature vary with time?", more specifically its narrowed question whether the gravitational coefficient G should equal the usual constant G0 only in the static state and otherwise vary according to the section’s stated rules while reproducing three benchmark phenomena. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft correctly captures (i) the section-level issue of whether a fundamental constant varies, (ii) the paper’s immediate specialization to the gravitational constant G, (iii) the contrast between a static state and nonstatic cases, and (iv) the demand for a specific rule checked against astronomical and laboratory-style examples. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))
missing_details: The paper’s official target is not a general theory of all constants: the title is broad, but the section immediately narrows to whether the gravitational constant G may vary. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))
The paper fixes the static-state value as G0, explicitly identified with the usual Newtonian gravitational constant 6.67×10^-11 N·m^2/kg^2. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))

The intended nonstatic question is posed under the added restriction that gravity still be written in inverse-square form; the variation is absorbed into a changing gravitational coefficient G. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))

The main rule derived from the improved gravitation formula is Eq. (62): G = G0(1 + 3G0Mp/(c^2r^2)). Your draft says only "according to a reproducible rule" but does not state the paper’s rule. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))

The variables in Eq. (62) must be defined: M and m are the two masses, r is their separation, c is the speed of light, and p is the half normal chord of the trajectory of m about M. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))
The paper also specifies p by orbit type: p = a(1-e^2) for an ellipse, p = a(e^2-1) for a hyperbola, and p = y^2/(2x) for a parabola. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))

The examples to be reproduced are not open-ended; they are exactly Mercury’s perihelion advance, gravitational deflection of a photon orbit around the sun, and a small ball moving down a long incline on Earth’s surface. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))
For Mercury, the stated range is (1 + 5.038109×10^-8)G0 ≤ G ≤ (1 + 1.162308×10^-7)G0. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))
For solar light deflection, the stated range is G0 ≤ G ≤ 2.5G0. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))
For the inclined-ball example, the constant-dimension-fractal model gives G = G0r^0.00011 and 1.001725G0 ≤ G ≤ 1.001735G0. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))

For the same inclined-ball example, the variable-dimension-fractal model gives F = -G0Mm/r^(2-δ), δ = 1.206×10^-12x, F = ma^(1+ε), ε = 8.779×10^-8x, x = 0 at the beginning static state, and hence G = G0r^δ with G0 ≤ G ≤ 1.000012G0. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))

Although the section title speaks of variation "with time," the formulas actually make G depend on dynamical/geometric quantities such as r, p, and x rather than on an explicit time variable t; a stand-alone question should reflect the paper’s actual formulation rather than introduce a time-law not stated there. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))
refined_question: In the sense of §7.7 of the paper, should one treat the gravitational coefficient as the usual constant G0 = 6.67×10^-11 N·m^2/kg^2 only in the static state, and in all other cases replace Newton’s law by an inverse-square law F = -GMm/r^2 with a state-dependent coefficient G determined from the paper’s improved gravitation formula by G = G0(1 + 3G0Mp/(c^2r^2)), where M and m are the two masses, r is their separation, c is the speed of light, and p is the half normal chord of the orbit of m about M (p = a(1-e^2) for an ellipse, p = a(e^2-1) for a hyperbola, p = y^2/(2x) for a parabola), and does this proposed rule reproduce the paper’s three benchmark cases with the stated bounds: Mercury’s perihelion advance, (1 + 5.038109×10^-8)G0 ≤ G ≤ (1 + 1.162308×10^-7)G0; gravitational deflection of a photon orbit around the sun, G0 ≤ G ≤ 2.5G0; and a small ball moving down a long incline on Earth’s surface, either via the constant-dimension-fractal relation G = G0r^0.00011 giving 1.001725G0 ≤ G ≤ 1.001735G0 or via the variable-dimension-fractal relation G = G0r^δ with δ = 1.206×10^-12x, x = 0 at the beginning static state, giving G0 ≤ G ≤ 1.000012G0? ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, can the paper’s improved universal gravitation formula F = -G0Mm/r^2 - (3G0^2M^2mp)/(c^2r^4) be re-expressed as an inverse-square law F = -GMm/r^2 with a variable gravitational coefficient, in which case the paper derives G = G0(1 + 3G0Mp/(c^2r^2))? ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))
justification: The draft is pointing to §7.7 rather than to neighboring material: the section title is exactly "Do fundamental constants in Nature vary with time?", but the opening paragraph immediately narrows the discussion to whether the gravitational constant G may vary. The reproduced abstract then gives the paper’s actual claim-shape: Newton’s law is retained with G = G0 in the static state; for "other cases" one insists on inverse-square form and introduces a changing gravitational coefficient G; and the proposal is checked against exactly three examples, not against a generic body of astronomical and laboratory data. The refined question therefore stays narrow by encoding the paper’s own rule, variables, and benchmark ranges instead of broadening it to all constants or to an unspecified time-varying law. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))
